items.prompt: Describe two methods of water supply.
items.canonical_answer: A reservoir behind a dam stores river water, which is then treated and piped to towns, so a seasonal flow becomes a year-round supply. A borehole is drilled into water-bearing rock and pumped, which supplies a town or a cluster of farms without a river nearby.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, to 2: each method named and its characteristic given - reservoir/dam, well/borehole, or desalination. The point or fact must say what the method does, not only its name.

items.prompt: Explain how water reaches users from a reservoir behind a dam.
items.canonical_answer: The dam blocks a river and the water backs up into a storage reservoir, which holds the wet season's flow. Water is released from the reservoir and piped or channelled to a treatment works, where it is filtered and disinfected. Clean water is then pumped through mains into homes, farms and factories, so the supply reaches users far from the river itself.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: how the water is stored behind the dam; because it is then treated before use; so it is piped or pumped to the users. The sequence of storage, treatment and delivery is the cause of the supply.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.6 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows approximate shares of fresh water used in two countries (rounded):

| use | Country A (low-income) / per cent | Country B (high-income) / per cent |
|---|---|---|
| agriculture | 80 | 40 |
| domestic | 10 | 15 |
| industry | 10 | 45 |

Describe the differences the table shows.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows agriculture taking by far the largest share in Country A - 80 per cent, twice Country B's 40 - while industry is Country B's largest use at 45 per cent against 10 per cent in Country A. Domestic use differs least: 10 and 15 per cent. The pattern means Country A's water goes to farming, while Country B spreads its use between industry and a fully plumbed population.
marking_guidance: Reading: the differences read from the table - the agricultural share and the industrial share, in both countries (1 mark).
Figures: the values quoted, so each difference is supported by the figures (1 mark).
The overall pattern drawn: the two economies' uses compared, which means the table is interpreted rather than listed (1 mark).

items.prompt: Asked how a dam and reservoir scheme supplies water to a city, a learner writes: "The dam was completed in 1998. It cost a lot and the president opened it. The dam is large." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has added background about the project's history instead of developing how the water reaches the users, so nothing in the answer supplies the city. A correct answer follows the water from source to user: the reservoir stores the river's flow, water is treated at the works, and mains carry it to homes and factories. In fact the date, cost and opening answer a different question from the one asked.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - background facts about the project, not how the water is supplied, which is a mistake of angle, not of fact.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - the answer follows the water: stored, treated, piped to the users.

items.prompt: A fast-growing town of 200 000 people sits on a dry plain. The nearest large river is 60 kilometres away, rainfall comes in three summer months, and many households fill containers from a polluted stream at the edge of town. Suggest three reasons why the town has a water shortage.
items.canonical_answer: The rainfall is seasonal, so for most of the year the local sources hold little water, which suggests the shortage is built into the town's climate. The town is growing fast, so demand from new households rises each year beyond what local wells and streams can supply. And the built supply that would carry river water 60 kilometres - pipelines, pumps and treatment works - appears not to exist yet, which means water that could relieve the shortage stays out of reach.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: each reason rests on this example - the seasonal rain, the growth in demand, or the missing link to the distant river - and is linked with because or so. Suggestions must fit the resource given.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.6 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A farming district loses about 40 per cent of the water pumped from its reservoir to leaking pipes, and flood irrigation is used on all its farms. Suggest which single change the district should make first to secure its future water supplies, and justify the choice.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement: repair the leaking delivery network first. The evidence is the figure: 40 per cent of the pumped water is lost before anyone uses it, so nearly half the supply the district already pays to collect and treat is being thrown away; mending leaks recovers that water at once, without building anything new. Switching the farms to drip irrigation would also save water, but it changes farm by farm and takes seasons to roll out. Since the largest single waste is measurable in the pipes themselves, the repair is the better first decision, with irrigation change to follow.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision - which change first (1 mark).
Because: the choice justified against the evidence given - the 40 per cent loss set against the slower, farm-by-farm irrigation change (1 mark).
So the answer weighs both options and commits, using the data in the stem; credit any reasoned decision backed by the figures (1 mark).

items.prompt:
The table shows a reservoir town's figures for two years:

| measure | 2015 | 2022 |
|---|---|---|
| population / thousands | 90 | 130 |
| annual rainfall / mm | 420 | 410 |
| water supplied per person per day / litres | 180 | 120 |

Describe what the table shows about the town's water supply.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows population rising steeply, from 90 thousand to 130 thousand, while rainfall barely changed, 420 millimetres to 410 - so the demand grew against a supply that did not. Water supplied per person fell from 180 litres a day to 120, which means each resident now has a third less than in 2015. The pattern shows a town outgrowing its water: the shortage is driven by growth, not by a change in the weather.
marking_guidance: Reading: the three trends read from the table - population up, rainfall steady, supply per person down (1 mark).
Figures: the values quoted for both years, so each trend is supported by the figures (1 mark).
The pattern connected: growth identified as the cause, which means the values are interpreted rather than repeated (1 mark).

items.prompt: Asked why a district has a water shortage, a learner writes: "The water is polluted, so people get sick from drinking it." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has explained why the water is unsafe when the question asks why it is scarce, and the two are not the same problem. A shortage is too little water: low rainfall, distant rivers or missing pipes and boreholes. Poor quality is polluted or untreated water, which can be plentiful and still harm people. In fact the correct answer here names how little water reaches the district, not what is wrong with the water that does.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - unsafe water explained instead of scarce water, which is not the same question.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - a shortage means too little water, with a cause such as low rainfall or a missing supply named.

items.prompt: Asked how a village's water supply could be improved, a learner writes: "The area needs better infrastructure." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The word infrastructure names nothing, so the answer cannot be judged or acted on - it is a label where a list of structures is needed. The correct answer names what would be built: a borehole with a hand pump, a pipeline from the river scheme, a small treatment works, a storage tank on the hill above the village. The test: what exactly would be built?
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the bare word used instead of naming what would be built, which leaves the answer empty.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - named structures: pipelines, pumps, treatment works, reservoirs or boreholes.

items.prompt: For Windhoek, Namibia's capital, describe two features of the city's water supply.
items.canonical_answer: The city draws water from boreholes into aquifers and from the Goreangab and Avis dams on small seasonal rivers, in a city whose rainfall is roughly 300-400 millimetres a year. And Windhoek runs a direct re-use plant that treats waste water and returns it to the drinking taps, the oldest such plant in continuous use worldwide.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, to 2: each a characteristic of Windhoek's supply - the boreholes, the two dams, the 300-400 mm rainfall, or the re-use plant. A general point about cities earns nothing.

items.prompt: For Windhoek, explain how the city manages its scarce water.
items.canonical_answer: Tariffs rise with the amount used, so heavy consumers pay more per litre, which was central to cutting the city's consumption in the 2016 drought year. The re-use plant treats waste water and returns it to the taps, so a litre drawn once serves the city twice, which is a large saving in a city with about 450 000 people and 300-400 millimetres of rain a year. Boreholes are pumped within measured limits, so the aquifers are drawn down slowly and recover in wetter years. Together the steps mean a dry capital keeps its taps through metering, recycling and restraint rather than through new dams.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per developed point, to 4: each step uses this example - the rising tariffs and the 2016 drought, the re-use plant, the measured borehole limits - and is linked with because or so to the effect it has on supply. Points that would fit any city, without Windhoek's detail, earn less.

items.prompt: For a named town or city, describe its water supply and explain how the supply is managed so that it meets people's needs. [7]
items.canonical_answer:
Windhoek, Namibia's capital, supplies about 450 000 people (mid-2010s, rounded) on the Central Plateau, one of the driest parts of the country, with roughly 300-400 millimetres of rain a year, nearly all in summer. The sources are boreholes into aquifers beneath and beside the city, the Goreangab and Avis dams on small seasonal rivers, and the direct re-use plant that treats waste water and returns it to the drinking taps - the oldest such plant in continuous use worldwide.

The supply is managed in steps. Tariffs rise with use, so the more a household consumes the more each litre costs, and these tariffs were central to cutting consumption in the drought year of 2016. The re-use plant recycles waste water, so a litre drawn once serves the city twice, stretching every borehole and dam. The boreholes are pumped within measured limits, so the aquifers are drawn down slowly and recover in wetter years. Together the steps show a dry capital keeping its taps through metering, recycling and restraint.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about dams or pipes, with no named example or only general points about water.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named place, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - Windhoek and its 450 000 people, the 300-400 mm rainfall, the Goreangab and Avis dams, the boreholes, the re-use plant and the 2016 tariffs - covering both the description and the management.

items.prompt:
The table shows approximate water use in a low-income country (Country A) and a high-income country (Country B), rounded:

| use | Country A / per cent | Country B / per cent |
|---|---|---|
| agriculture | 80 | 40 |
| domestic | 10 | 15 |
| industry | 10 | 45 |
| water used per person per day / litres | 50 | 300 |

(a) Identify the largest use of water in Country B. [1]
(b) Describe two differences in water use between the two countries shown by the table. [2]
(c) Suggest why Country A's agriculture takes such a large share of the country's water. [3]
(d) Suggest two strategies that could reduce waste in Country B's domestic water use. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Industry.
(b) Country A's largest use is agriculture at 80 per cent - double Country B's 40 per cent - while Country B's largest is industry at 45 per cent against 10 per cent in Country A. Water used per person also differs by six times: 50 litres a day against 300.
(c) Farming dominates the economy and needs irrigation in dry seasons, so most water is channelled to crops. Industry is small, so it draws little, which leaves agriculture with the largest share. And much farming is in dry regions where nothing grows without watering, so the irrigation demand is high.
(d) Metering with rising tariffs would make each household's use visible, which typically cuts waste. And repairing leaks in the delivery network would save water that has already been collected and treated, since a piped system that loses a large share never delivers it.
marking_guidance: Resource: parts (a) and (b) are read from the table - 1 mark for the use identified; 2 marks for two differences, each backed by the figures from the resource.
Marks: part (c) is worth 3 marks - three reasons suggested for the agricultural share, each linked to irrigation, the economy's shape or the dry climate; credit reasons that fit the data.
Figures: part (d) is worth 2 marks - two strategies for domestic use, developed with their effect, such as metering or leak repair; strategies for farming do not answer the question asked.
